title: Split the money, keep the average
hook: Does spreading money across bets cost you returns? Or just risk?

knows: expected value: the average result over many tries
that two coin flips can land four ways
doesNotKnow: that splitting across independent bets cuts the chance of the worst outcomes without changing the average
that this depends on the bets being independent

misconception: Splitting your money must lower what you expect to make.
objective: The learner can explain that splitting money across independent bets leaves the average unchanged while making extreme outcomes rarer, because the bets partly cancel, and that this needs independence.

claims.text: With two independent bets you lose only if both fall: ½ × ½ = 25% (split equally across two independent bets that each pay +20% or −10% with equal chance, the loss is −10%).
claims.source: outcomes(2): returns −10%, +5%, +20% with chances 1/4, 1/2, 1/4; only −10% is a loss. Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14. v5: the stage no longer pins itself to 2 bets; the 25% is in the 'Chance of a loss seen' row (milestone two-bets).

claims.text: Half the time one bet rises and one falls, for +5%.
The average stays +5% however many bets the money is split across.
claims.source: Each bet's expected return is 0.5 × 20 + 0.5 × (−10) = 5; an equal split's expected return is the average of the bets' expected returns, 5, for every n. Demo.tsx average(n) enumerates the binomial outcomes.

claims.text: The worst case, every bet falling (−10%), has chance 50%, 25%, 12.5%… halving with each added bet.
The chance of some loss does not fall at every step: with 4 bets it was 31.3%, more than the 25% with 2. (Shown in the reveal only if the learner visited 4 bets.)
claims.source: outcomes(4): returns −10, −2.5, +5, +12.5, +20 with chances 1, 4, 6, 4, 1 /16; losses −10 and −2.5 give 5/16 = 31.25%, which pct() renders 31.3%. Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14.

claims.text: A model with made-up numbers. Real investments often fall together. Not advice.
claims.source: Disclosure. The numbers (+20% / −10%, equal chance) are invented. That real assets' returns are often positively correlated is general context; the lesson's own evidence for what correlation does is the 'together' state on stage (c9), not an external source.

claims.text: Independent bets partly cancel: as you split further the bars bunch around +5%, and the worst case, every bet falling, gets rarer.
claims.source: Binomial: the spread of the average return shrinks like 1/sqrt(n); the worst case has chance 1/2^n (c4). Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14, for n = 1..6.

claims.text: Chart labels: the 0% bar is labelled 'break even'; every bar has a return tick under it (e.g. −10%, 0%, +10%, +20% at 3 bets).
claims.source: outcomes(n) in Demo.tsx: returns (k × 20 + (n − k) × (−10)) / n for k = 0..n; at n = 3 these are −10, 0, +10, +20. A 0% result is neither gain nor loss (lossChance counts r < 0 only). | REVISED v4 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, wave D r5): new sentence. New stage text (r5 minor). | FC pass 22 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): node outcomes(3): -10, 0, +10, +20; ticks are every bar's return (plus a 0% tick only when no bar is within 4 points: n = 1, 2). 'break even' label on r === 0 bars (n = 3, 6; exact zeros in floating point).

claims.text: When the bets move together, any split loses 50% of the time, the same as one bet; splitting only cancels risk when the bets do not fall together.
claims.source: Perfectly correlated bets all return the same, so an equal split returns +20% or −10% with chance 1/2 each, whatever n (Demo.tsx outcomes(n, 'together')). This is the extreme case (correlation 1); for partly correlated bets the cancelling is partial. Builder's derivation, 2026-10-14.

recall.question: You split money equally between two independent bets with the same average return. Compared with putting it all in one, what changes?
options: The average stays the same; the worst outcome gets rarer
recall.why: Each bet has the same average, so the split does too. Both have to go badly for the worst case, which is less likely than one going badly.
